blocking_rules.description: The surname sounds the same and both parts of the date of birth agree. This is the rule that finds most pairs.
blocking_rules.sql: l.surname_metaphone = r.surname_metaphone AND l.dob_year_clean = r.dob_year_clean AND l.dob_month_clean = r.dob_month_clean
blocking_rules._measured: The earlier engine measured 19.2 million pairs over 5.16 million representatives. This is the rule the pair budget is sized for.

blocking_rules.description: The first three letters of the surname, the forename initial and the date of birth all agree. This catches a surname the sound key splits.
blocking_rules.sql: substr(l.surname_clean, 1, 3) = substr(r.surname_clean, 1, 3) AND l.forename_initial = r.forename_initial AND l.dob_year_clean = r.dob_year_clean AND l.dob_month_clean = r.dob_month_clean

blocking_rules.description: The sorted letters of the forename and surname agree. This catches a filing that carries a middle name against one that does not.
Same postcode district and the surname sounds the same. This rescues a pair a mistyped date of birth would have hidden from the first rule.
The forename sound and the date of birth agree while the surname sound does not. This is the rule that finds a changed surname.
blocking_rules.sql: l.forename_metaphone = r.forename_metaphone AND l.dob_year_clean = r.dob_year_clean AND l.dob_month_clean = r.dob_month_clean AND l.surname_metaphone <> r.surname_metaphone
blocking_rules._measured: The earlier engine measured its routes catching 42.9% of 37,467 verified surname-change pairs, and this rule lifting that to 67.2%.

blocking_rules.description: Both name sounds agree and at least one side has no usable birth year, so the first rule could never have seen the pair.
blocking_rules.sql: l.surname_metaphone = r.surname_metaphone AND l.forename_metaphone = r.forename_metaphone AND (l.dob_year_clean IS NULL OR r.dob_year_clean IS NULL)

comparisons.description: Surname. A rare surname counts for more than a common one, so agreeing on FOTHERGILL is stronger evidence than agreeing on SMITH.
Forename after the nickname lookup, so ROBERT and BOB have already met.
Middle names. Most filings carry none, so most pairs land on the null level and are neither helped nor punished.

Birth year, graded by how far apart the two years are: equal, within one year, then anything else. A gap of two years or more has a level of its own, so the engine can learn what that gap is worth. A rare year does not count for more than a common one, because these levels are gaps between years, not years.
comparisons._measured: The old two-level comparison could not express '37 years apart' at all. Fitting it on data full of different people who share a name left a disagreement costing almost nothing, so the score could not fall far enough to keep two people apart.

comparisons.description: Birth month, exact. Compared separately from the year so that agreeing on both is two pieces of evidence and disagreeing on either costs something.
Nationality, with the home nations collapsed into one. A rare nationality counts for more than a common one, so agreeing on LATVIAN says more than agreeing on BRITISH.
Postcode at full, sector, district and area level. Formation-agent postcodes are already nulled by the cleaning, which is what makes this safe to score on at all.
comparisons._measured: Term frequency was off here and on for the surname, and on the full run that single asymmetry is why a shared postcode DISTRICT learned +9.26 bits against a shared surname's +9.33. The learned u is not the problem: measured over the run's own 11,205,785 person units, the true random-pair rate for a district match is 0.000543 against the 0.000575 the model learned — 5.9% out, and in the direction that UNDERSTATES the weight. A UK postcode district really is about as rare as a UK surname (1,342 effective districts against 2,211 effective surnames, because SMITH, KHAN, JONES, SINGH and PATEL alone cover 1.4 million person units). What is wrong is that the surname weight is individualised and the postcode weight is not: agreeing on SMITH is worth 5.53 bits after the adjustment, while agreeing on E14 — which is as common as JONES — is worth a flat 9.26. Turning term frequency on here individualises the FULL postcode level, which is the strongest one. It cannot individualise the sector, district or area levels: cl.PostcodeComparison builds those by regular expression over postcode_clean and Splink can only attach a frequency table to the exact-match level, so the flat district weight stands until a custom postcode comparison is built the way custom.NumericDifferenceAtThresholds was. THE FULL RUN HAS NOT BEEN RESCORED WITH THIS CHANGE.

em_blocking_rules.sql: l.dob_year_clean = r.dob_year_clean AND l.dob_month_clean = r.dob_month_clean AND l.postcode_district = r.postcode_district

person._lost_in_translation: deduping used three custom comparison ladders. (1) dob_joint is now BUILT: dob_year_clean is a custom.NumericDifferenceAtThresholds with thresholds [0, 1] — equal, within 1, all other — and the month stays a separate exact comparison, so agreeing on both is two pieces of evidence. (2) address_freq: postcode levels split by how many records share that postcode (rare <=20, mid <=1000, then district). cl.PostcodeComparison has the geographic ladder but not the frequency split; the junk-postcode nullify removes the worst of it and the model sees postcode_equal and postcode_district_equal. (3) Every comparison there ended in a fixed neutral else with the EM output clamped so no interior level could become a penalty; this document has no clamp, so a level CAN learn a penalty here.
person._em_note: Two rules on purpose. Splink cannot estimate a comparison whose columns the training rule holds equal, so one rule fixes the name sounds (and estimates the date of birth, nationality and postcode) and the other fixes the date of birth (and estimates the names). With the single name+DOB rule this file shipped with, dob_year_clean came back m=None on every level: the comparison was dead weight, and pairs 37 birth-years apart scored 1.0.
person._em_cost_note: The second rule carries postcode_district as well, and it is there for cost, not for accuracy. Year plus month alone is far too coarse to block on: it puts 449,397 sample units into 1,058 blocks and makes 170,613,604 training pairs, against 2.4M for the whole of prediction. That is what hung the first re-score — 53 GB of DuckDB spill and a 40-minute timeout. Adding the district takes it to 165,464 pairs over 331,596 blocks while still leaving both name comparisons free to be estimated, which is the rule's whole purpose. It covers 418,915 of 449,397 person units (93.2%); the rest have no postcode and simply do not train this rule. The budget check now prices em_blocking_rules too, so a regression here fails the run instead of hanging it. AT FULL SCALE BOTH RULES NEED THE HOT-KEY CONTROL, and that is why an em_blocking_rule may now carry one. On the 2026-09-18 snapshot's 11,205,785 person units the first rule makes 582,535,879 training pairs uncontrolled - three and a half times the 170M rule that spilled 53 GB and hung a whole session, and about 180 GB of spill at the 312 bytes a pair those two retain_ flags cost. With on_oversize 'drop' over 60 it is 43,054,672, and the second rule is 105,630,616 uncontrolled and 58,985,721 controlled. No refine column is used, so nothing is held equal that was not held equal before and both guards stay clean. What is dropped from TRAINING is the placeholder-name hot blocks of PSC_HANDOVER.md section 19; prediction still sees those units under its own control, and a model should not be learning its weights from FLTS and PRSNS.
person._block_control_note: Every route refines an oversized block on postcode_district, which is the one column independent of a name-sound or date-of-birth key; pb4 already fixes the district and refines on the date of birth instead. Priced on the full 2026-09-18 snapshot's 11,205,785 person units: the six routes fall from 1,901,943,106 pairs to 94,743,605, and each one drops about 79,000 units as too common to compare on that rule. on_oversize 'drop' alone would cut slightly more and cost pb5 4,720,900 units - 42% of the track - which is why it is refine and not drop. PSC_HANDOVER.md section 104.

blocking_rules.description: Same core-name sound and the same kind of body, so a GmbH and a trust of similar name are not compared.
Same registration number, whatever the name says.
Same first word of the core name and the same postcode district: a renamed company at one address.

comparisons.description: The name with the legal form split off. The main signal on this track.
Sorted distinct words of the core name, on overlap. Catches a different word order and a dropped word.
Registration number. Strong when it is there; the match keys have usually taken these already.
Country of registration as a short code.
What kind of body it is. Weak alone; it mainly keeps a trust apart from a company of the same name.
Postcode at full, sector, district and area level.

organisation._em_note: Two rules, so no comparison is held equal by all of them. With only the name+type rule, type_bucket never varied inside the training block and came back untrained — the same silent failure the person track had.
organisation._block_control_note: Same control, refining on postcode_district except ob4, whose key already fixes it and which refines on type_bucket. 164,706,223 pairs to 1,832,607 over 593,640 units.
organisation._em_cost_note: Both rules carry the same hot-key control. On the full snapshot's 593,640 organisation units they are 48,450,086 and 26,960,626 pairs uncontrolled and 639,077 and 349,935 with on_oversize 'drop' over 60.

_budget_note: max_pairs is sized from the priced full-snapshot total with about 1.5x headroom: the person track's six routes make at most 94,743,605 blocked comparisons after the hot-key control, and its worst EM training rule 58,985,721 after its own, so 150,000,000 covers both with room. The organisation track's routes make 1,832,607 and its worst EM rule 639,077, so 5,000,000 is already generous. Both figures are linkage.price_rule group arithmetic on the run's own units.parquet, confirmed against Splink's own count_comparisons_from_blocking_rule before the run. PSC_HANDOVER.md section 104.
_postcode_district_conjunction_measured: The fourth clause is a conjunction: it holds a cluster only when BOTH counts are over their limits. A limit on postcode districts alone is wrong, and measurably so. On the full run, of the twenty person entities with more than five districts, fourteen are one real person with several companies at several registered offices — Blažena Murgacova has 17 districts, one birth date and one name; Xuemei Gong has 10. A district-only gate at 5 would hold 14,221 entities and 183,033 records, about seven in ten of them right. Raised to 8 it holds 1,899 entities and catches none of the four genuinely wrong ones in the sample. The signal is the BIRTH DATE, not the address: 'more than one distinct birth date' flags exactly the four wrong entities and the two doubtful ones and none of the fourteen right ones, six for six and fourteen for fourteen. The two together hold 3,596 entities and 45,151 records, and they catch both known bad entities — PSCP-0001415599 (Mohammed/Muhammad Imran, 75 records, 36 districts, 9 birth dates) and PSCP-0001416257 (46 records, 22 districts, 5 birth dates). The birth date is counted as the year and the month TOGETHER, as one value, because PSC units carry dob_year_clean and dob_month_clean and no combined column, and the combining belongs to the gate rather than to a new cleaning step. Report: psc_person_evidence_2026-09-22.md, section 2.
_max_distinct_values_measured: The cluster gate had no equivalent of the match keys' max_distinct guard, and it showed: on the full run too_large fired on 17 person clusters and missed all twenty of the largest proposed person entities, one of which held 217 records under 165 distinct names. Counted over that run's own clusters, a person cluster of two units carries at most 2 distinct cleaned surnames and averages 1.11; one of 6 to 20 units averages 2.33; one of over 100 units averages 104. Sampled at 4 to 8 distinct surnames, every cluster was a mixture. Three is the most one person can honestly show: a birth name, a married name, and one inconsistently filed hyphenated variant. THE FORENAME IS HERE BECAUSE THE SURNAME WAS NOT ENOUGH: with the surname gated and the new veto rules in, the twelve largest remaining wrong person entities were all one surname and many forenames — 206 records under 55 names, every one of them Singh, and the same for Khan, Mia and Ali. A chain that cannot run away on the surname runs away on the forename instead. The organisation track names no column, so it is not gated this way, and neither is donations, where a trade union's branches legitimately carry many different names. THE BIRTH YEAR IS HERE FOR THE SAME REASON, ONE STEP ON: with the surname and the forename both gated, the largest wrong person entities left were 111 records under 57 names, every one of them 'Mohammed <something> Ali', spread over 29 different birth years. The chain runs away on the middle name and the year instead. A person has one birth year, and v1 leaves one year of slack for a filing slip, so a cluster can honestly show two adjacent years; three or more is a chain. Counted on the full run's own person clusters, 1,713,278 show one birth year and 36,156 show two, against 2,037 that show more than two — one tenth of one per cent, and a clean break in the data.
